questions.Source/Guideline: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
questions.Question: A 63-year-old man has favorable intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer, minimal pattern 4 disease, low PSA density, and strong preference to defer treatment toxicity. What initial management discussion is most appropriate?
questions.Option A: Watchful waiting because any intermediate-risk disease is incurable
questions.Option B: Active surveillance, radiation therapy, and radical prostatectomy
questions.Option D: Whole-gland ablation as the proven superior standard
questions.Option E: Immediate pelvic nodal radiation without prostate treatment
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Favorable intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer can be managed with a discussion of active surveillance, radiation therapy, and radical prostatectomy when tumor features and patient priorities fit. Option A is incorrect because watchful waiting is mainly for limited life expectancy rather than a blanket intermediate-risk rule. Option C is incorrect because ADT alone is not definitive curative treatment for this scenario. Option D is incorrect because ablation lacks high-quality comparative outcome data against established options. Option E is incorrect because elective nodal radiation alone does not treat the prostate cancer. Teaching point: Favorable intermediate-risk disease is preference-sensitive, but the choice set still has to match oncologic risk. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
questions.Question: A man elects radical prostatectomy for unfavorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. Estimated lymph node risk is high enough to justify node staging. What pelvic lymphadenectomy counseling is most accurate?
questions.Option A: It consistently improves metastasis-free and overall survival
questions.Option B: It should be omitted because imaging was negative
questions.Option C: A limited dissection is preferred for staging accuracy
questions.Option D: It provides staging information, and nomograms should guide selection
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. Pelvic lymphadenectomy provides staging information that can guide later management, and nomograms should be used to select patients by balancing nodal-yield benefit against complications. Option A is incorrect because consistent survival improvement has not been documented. Option B is incorrect because negative imaging does not by itself eliminate the value of surgical staging in selected patients. Option C is incorrect because an extended dissection improves staging accuracy compared with limited dissection when lymphadenectomy is performed. Option E is incorrect because pathologic staging does not replace PSA follow-up. Teaching point: Pelvic lymphadenectomy is a staging tool selected by risk, not a default therapeutic guarantee. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A complete TURBT shows a 3 cm high-risk high-grade Ta urothelial carcinoma with muscle present and no perforation. Which next resection step should be considered?
questions.Option B: Radical cystectomy as routine immediate treatment
questions.Option C: No cystoscopic reassessment until one year
questions.Option D: Repeat TURBT of the primary tumor site within six weeks
questions.Option E: Upper-tract ureteroscopy as the next bladder staging step
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. For high-risk, high-grade Ta tumors, repeat transurethral resection of the primary tumor site within six weeks should be considered because residual tumor and staging uncertainty can change management. Option A is incorrect because office fulguration is not adequate restaging for high-grade Ta disease. Option B is incorrect because cystectomy is not routine immediate treatment for a completely resected high-grade Ta tumor. Option C is incorrect because waiting one year ignores early residual disease risk. Option E is incorrect because upper-tract ureteroscopy does not restage the bladder tumor bed. Teaching point: High-grade Ta is noninvasive, but it is not low-stakes Ta. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent calcium stone former continues to form stones despite diet changes, but repeat 24-hour urine testing shows no persistent hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, or hyperuricosuria. What medication strategy is guideline-aligned?
questions.Option A: No medication can be used without a urine abnormality
questions.Option B: Acetohydroxamic acid as empiric calcium stone prevention
questions.Option D: Empiric alpha blocker therapy for prevention
questions.Option E: Thiazide diuretic or potassium citrate therapy
questions.Explanation: Option E is correct. Thiazide diuretics and/or potassium citrate may be offered to recurrent calcium stone formers when other metabolic abnormalities are absent or have been addressed but stone formation persists. Option A is incorrect because empiric directed prevention can still be appropriate after recurrent events. Option B is incorrect because acetohydroxamic acid is for selected struvite stones after surgical options are exhausted. Option C is incorrect because antibiotics do not prevent metabolic calcium stones. Option D is incorrect because alpha blockers may help selected ureteral stone passage but do not prevent recurrent renal calcium stones. Teaching point: Recurrent calcium stone prevention can be phenotype-driven even when the 24-hour urine is not diagnostic. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent calcium stone former starts chlorthalidone for high urinary calcium. Which follow-up plan best addresses medication safety?
questions.Option A: No laboratory monitoring is needed after thiazide initiation
questions.Option C: Periodic blood testing for drug adverse effects
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. Pharmacologic stone prevention requires follow-up that includes periodic blood testing to detect adverse effects such as thiazide-associated electrolyte changes. Option A is incorrect because thiazides can cause clinically relevant metabolic adverse effects. Option B is incorrect because urine cytology is unrelated to calcium stone medication monitoring. Option D is incorrect because imaging may still be needed to follow stone activity. Option E is incorrect because cystoscopy is not part of thiazide safety monitoring. Teaching point: Preventive stone medication is not a one-time prescription; response and toxicity both need follow-up. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A 69-year-old woman with idiopathic OAB and blood pressure 186/112 mm Hg asks to start mirabegron today. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
questions.Option A: Mirabegron is preferred because hypertension does not affect selection
questions.Option B: Mirabegron should be avoided until severe uncontrolled hypertension is addressed
questions.Option C: Urodynamics is required to prove detrusor overactivity before medication
questions.Option D: Chronic urethral catheterization is first-line therapy
questions.Option E: Urine cytology determines beta-3 agonist eligibility
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Mirabegron is not recommended in patients with severe uncontrolled hypertension, so blood pressure control and an alternative OAB plan should be addressed before prescribing it. Option A is incorrect because severe uncontrolled hypertension directly affects mirabegron selection. Option C is incorrect because urodynamic confirmation is not required before medication in uncomplicated idiopathic OAB. Option D is incorrect because chronic urethral catheterization is not first-line OAB therapy. Option E is incorrect because urine cytology has no role in beta-3 agonist eligibility. Teaching point: Beta-3 agonists are useful OAB medications, but drug-specific safety constraints still matter. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A woman with idiopathic OAB had inadequate durable response to intradetrusor botulinum toxin and wants another minimally invasive option rather than a chronic catheter. Which option is supported?
questions.Option B: Long-term urethral Foley as routine next therapy
questions.Option D: Annual CT urograms for urgency control
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. Sacral neuromodulation can be used for patients with inadequately controlled OAB symptoms, including after inadequate response to or intolerance of botulinum toxin. Option B is incorrect because chronic catheterization is a last-resort incontinence-management option and should not be routine next therapy. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy may evaluate selected diagnostic uncertainty but does not treat idiopathic OAB symptoms. Option D is incorrect because CT urography is not OAB therapy. Option E is incorrect because pelvic lymphadenectomy has no role in OAB management. Teaching point: Minimally invasive OAB options can be sequenced by response and patient preference without defaulting to chronic catheterization. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Question: A 34-year-old patient with no smoking history has confirmed microhematuria with 4 RBC/hpf, no gross hematuria, and no additional urothelial cancer risk factors. What is the next step?
questions.Option C: Urine cytology as the required first test
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. Low/negligible-risk microhematuria should be followed with repeat urinalysis within six months rather than immediate cystoscopy or imaging. Option B is incorrect because CT urography and cystoscopy are not the initial pathway for low/negligible-risk patients. Option C is incorrect because cytology is not required as the first test in this risk group. Option D is incorrect because intravesical chemotherapy requires a bladder cancer indication. Option E is incorrect because confirmed microhematuria still needs guideline-directed follow-up. Teaching point: Risk stratification prevents both missed evaluation and reflex over-testing. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

questions.Question: A 58-year-old man with a 12 pack-year smoking history has confirmed microhematuria with 18 RBC/hpf and no renal insufficiency. He is categorized as intermediate risk. What evaluation is recommended?
questions.Option A: Repeat dipstick alone in one year
questions.Option B: Urine cytology without imaging or cystoscopy
questions.Option E: No evaluation if culture is negative
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. Intermediate-risk microhematuria should be evaluated with cystoscopy and renal ultrasound. Option A is incorrect because repeat dipstick alone is inadequate after confirmed intermediate-risk microhematuria. Option B is incorrect because cytology alone cannot evaluate the bladder and upper tracts. Option D is incorrect because upper-tract imaging without cystoscopy misses the recommended bladder evaluation. Option E is incorrect because a negative culture does not eliminate the need for risk-based hematuria evaluation. Teaching point: Intermediate-risk microhematuria uses ultrasound rather than automatically escalating every patient to CT urography. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
questions.Question: A woman with recurrent cystitis symptoms has a voided culture reported as mixed vaginal flora with many epithelial cells. What is the best next diagnostic step before changing prophylaxis?
questions.Option A: Treat the mixed-flora result as definitive infection
questions.Option B: Repeat urine studies, considering a catheterized specimen
questions.Option D: Perform monthly CT urograms for culture clarification
questions.Option E: Ignore future symptoms because the culture was contaminated
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. When an initial urine specimen is suspicious for contamination, repeat urine studies should be obtained and a catheterized specimen can be considered to clarify culture results. Option A is incorrect because mixed vaginal flora and epithelial cells can reflect contamination rather than true infection. Option C is incorrect because lifelong fluoroquinolone suppression is excessive and unsafe without reliable microbiologic confirmation. Option D is incorrect because routine monthly CT urography is not part of recurrent uncomplicated UTI diagnosis. Option E is incorrect because symptoms still require accurate evaluation. Teaching point: Recurrent UTI management depends on linking symptoms to credible microbiology, not treating contaminated cultures. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
